lines.text: What if the Suez Canal, one thin ditch in Egypt, closed for a whole year?
In 2021, about 12% of the world's trade sailed through this one strip of water: phones, clothes, cars and oil.
It was dug through the desert and opened in 1869, so ships could skip the long way round Africa.
So a ship from China reaches Europe the short way: across the Indian Ocean, up the Red Sea and through the canal, into the Mediterranean.
So what happens when it is blocked? In 2021, one giant ship, the Ever Given, got stuck sideways across it, its nose in one bank and its tail in the other.
For 6 days, nothing moved, and ships piled up at both ends, in a queue you could see from space.
Now close it for a year. Where does every ship go? It turns around and takes the long way, past the tip of Africa.
Race the two routes, and the long way costs about 10 more days at sea on a trip from Asia to Europe, and a lot more fuel.
Remember, that one blockage held up about $9.6B of goods every day. Close it for a year, and that jam would never, ever end.
Suez or Panama: which shortcut would hurt the world more? Tell me down below in the comments. Now picture it one more time:
